title: Pfizer signs US$2.6B Starna deal to expand in vivo CAR-T pipeline in China | HealthCare Middle East & Africa - No.1 Health & Pharma Manufacturing Industry Publication

contentHtml:
CHINA— Pfizer has signed a licensing agreement worth up to US$2.63billion with biotechnology company Starna Therapeutics to develop in vivo CAR-T therapies for autoimmune diseases, expanding its presence in a growing area of cell therapy research.

Under the agreement, Pfizer will pay US$330million upfront for exclusive rights outside China to three in vivo CAR-T programmes.

Starna is also eligible to receive up to US$2.3billion in development and commercial milestone payments, alongside royalties on net sales of any resulting products.

Pfizer confirmed that all three programmes are at the pre-investigational new drug (pre-IND) stage but did not disclose further details about the drug candidates.

The agreement also grants Pfizer access to Starna’s proprietary in vivo CAR-T technology for applications in inflammation and immunology, as well as oncology.

In addition, the companies will establish a separate research collaboration under which Pfizer can exclusively license compounds developed through their joint work.

The agreement includes an option for Pfizer to expand its territorial rights to Greater China.

Pfizer targets next-generation CAR-T therapies

The partnership marks an expansion of Pfizer’s cell therapy strategy. The pharmaceutical company has previously pursued ex vivo CAR-T development through licensing agreements with Cellectis and Servier.

However, its latest move reflects growing industry interest in in vivo approaches, which could address some of the manufacturing and scalability challenges associated with conventional CAR-T treatments.

Unlike ex vivo CAR-T therapies, which require clinicians to collect a patient’s T cells, modify them in a laboratory and reinfuse them, in vivo approaches aim to genetically modify these immune cells directly inside the body.

This could simplify treatment delivery, reduce manufacturing requirements and potentially make CAR-T therapies more accessible.

Pfizer’s chief inflammation and immunology officer, Michael Vincent, said the approach could address unmet treatment needs among patients whose autoimmune conditions respond poorly to existing therapies.

He also highlighted the company’s experience in developing and manufacturing RNA-based medicines as an advantage in advancing Starna’s programmes.

The agreement comes amid increased investment in in vivo CAR-T technology.

Eli Lilly has made two major acquisitions in the field this year, spending US$2.4 billion to acquire Orna Therapeutics in February and US$7 billion to take over Kelonia in April.

Johnson & Johnson and Moderna have also pursued transactions targeting the modality.

China strengthens position in pharmaceutical innovation

Pfizer’s agreement also highlights the growing importance of Chinese biotechnology companies in global pharmaceutical research and development.

Earlier this week, Pfizer chief executive Albert Bourla discussed China’s expanding influence on drug innovation at the Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference in London on 17 November.

He noted that competition in the pharmaceutical industry is increasingly shifting beyond the traditional rivalry between Western multinational drugmakers, reflecting China’s growing contribution to drug development.

However, geopolitical considerations could influence how pharmaceutical companies pursue partnerships with Chinese biotechnology firms.

Although licensing agreements such as the Pfizer-Starna deal remain viable, tighter US national security policies could restrict other forms of cross-border investment and corporate transactions.
